How to Play

Five regions trade goods to get what they need. Here is how the game works, step by step.

How to Play: The Triangle Trade Unit 1 · Mr. B’s Social Studies

The goal

Be the first region to get everything on your secret needs list.

  • New England Home port: Boston 7 ships
  • Middle Colonies Home port: Philadelphia 2 ships
  • Southern Colonies Home port: Charleston No ships
  • West Indies Home port: Kingston No ships
  • England Home port: London 8 ships

The Southern Colonies and the West Indies have no ships. They must hire a ship or trade for one.

  • Your score = how much of your needs list you have.
  • Time's up and nobody finished? The highest score wins. A tie goes to the team with more voyages.

The build-up: five steps

  1. 1 ReadRead your region's reading on your own.Readings come in four levels.
  2. 2 Take notesFill in the Region Notes sheet.Products, needs, ships, who did the work, biggest advantage, biggest challenge.
  3. 3 Plan as a teamCopy your secret needs. Make a plan.Your monopolies, your ship plan, your first move.
  4. 4 TradePlay rounds: Negotiation, then Shipping.The teacher runs the clock.
  5. 5 Count up and reflectCount your goods. Then think:Was the Triangle Trade worth it, and to whom?

Your team's jobs

Captain 1 person

  • Carries out the deals in Shipping.
  • Takes the goods cards to the Dock. Draws a chance card each way.
  • Comes back to port quickly.

One person is the captain. During Shipping rounds, the captain carries out the deals. Fill out the ship's manifest (6 items at most), take it to the teacher's Dock, and draw a chance card for the trip out and another for the trip back. A Free Passage card can cancel one bad card later, but not an Admiralty Court inspection. Come back to port quickly, because only the merchant OR the captain can be away.

Merchant 1 person

  • The person in charge of trade.
  • In Negotiation, visits another port to offer a deal.
  • No goods move yet. A deal counts only when your Harbormasters say yes.

One person on the team is the merchant, the person in charge of trade. During Negotiation rounds, the merchant goes to other ports to learn what they have and need, and to offer deals. No goods move during Negotiation. A deal counts only after your harbormasters approve it.

Harbormasters everyone else

  • Stay at your home port the whole game.
  • Keep the record. Talk with visiting Merchants.
  • Vote on every deal. Each one also has a Harbormaster job.

Everyone on the team except the merchant and the captain is a harbormaster. Harbormasters stay at the home port the whole game. They keep the record of every item the region owns, gives, and gets. They talk with merchants who visit, and they vote on every deal. No trade is final until the harbormasters say yes. Each harbormaster has one job: Record Keeper (writes every deal and voyage in the trade log), Counter (counts the goods cards after each round), Port Negotiator (talks with visiting merchants), or Strategist (watches the board and plans the merchant's next visit).

Big rule: only the Merchant OR the Captain is away from port. Never both.

Harbormaster jobs

Every Harbormaster has one. Fewer than four Harbormasters? Double up.

  • Record Keeper Writes every deal and voyage in the trade log before the Captain leaves.
  • Counter Counts the goods cards at the end of each round, fills in “What we have” and ticks off needs.
  • Port Negotiator Meets visiting Merchants at your table and says what your team would accept.
  • Strategist Watches the board and your needs list. Decides the Merchant’s next target.

What's on your table

  1. Table tent: your region's name and home port.
  2. Goods cards: 28 cards in your region's color. Ships are cards too. Keep them in the bag.
  3. Harbormaster Record, one per team. Side 1: TOP SECRET needs and a count of what you have. Side 2: the trade log.
  4. Reading and Region Notes sheet, one each.

C Captain · M Merchant · H Harbormaster

A round, step by step

A round is Negotiation, then Shipping. Rounds repeat until the teacher calls time. Sometimes the teacher pauses the game to ask the whole class a question. That’s part of the game.

Negotiation about 3 minutes

  1. Merchant Walk to ONE other port.
  2. Merchant Offer a deal: what you give, what you get.
  3. Their Harbormasters They say yes or no.
  4. Merchant Come home. Tell your team.
  5. Your Harbormasters Vote yes or no. Write the deal in the trade log.
The game says: NEGOTIATION ROUND — Regions with a ship may send their merchant to one other port to propose a trade. Nothing changes hands yet — harbormasters must approve every deal.

Shipping about 5 minutes

  1. Harbormasters Pick up to 6 goods cards. Match the trade log.
  2. Captain Take the cards and the folded log to the Dock.
  3. Dock Chance card on the way out.
  4. Captain Deliver the goods. Load what comes back.
  5. Dock Chance card on the way home.
  6. Harbormasters Count your cards. Tick off your needs.
The game says: SHIPPING ROUND — Captains load up (6 items max) and physically carry the goods cards to the agreed port — but report to the Admiralty Dock for a chance card first.

The game's Negotiation rule: “NEGOTIATION ROUND — Regions with a ship may send their merchant to one other port to propose a trade. Nothing changes hands yet — harbormasters must approve every deal.”

Ships

  • A ship carries 6 goods at most, each way.
  • New England, the Middle Colonies and England own ships (New England 7, Middle Colonies 2, England 8).
  • No ship? Hire one: make a deal with a team that has ships. The fee rides as cargo: load the goods you pay with in the hold (they count toward the 6), and they go to the ship’s owner. The ship goes back to them.
  • Or trade for a ship card. Tell the teacher at the Dock, so the game moves the ship to you.
  • A ship can sail out empty to pick goods up, or come home empty after a delivery.

Chance cards

Two per voyage: one on the way out, one on the way home. The deck has 36 cards.

Good news 21 of 36

  • ×18 Favorable Winds Nothing happens. Sail on.
  • ×1 Free Passage! Keep it. Later it cancels one card that costs you goods. Not the Admiralty Court.
  • ×1 Lucky Winds! Add 1 good from home to the ship.
  • ×1 Governor's Favor Choose any port to visit next.

Lose cargo 9 of 36

  • Lose 1: Storm at Sea, Sprung a Leak
  • Lose 2: Pirates Spotted!, Bad Weather, Rough Seas, Ship Needs Repairs
  • Lose 3: Severe Storm!, Pirates Board Your Ship!, Fire Below Deck!

The Captain picks which goods.

Pay a duty 2 of 36

  • ×1 Customs Inspection Pay 1 good. They go to England.
  • ×1 British Tax Collector Pay 2 goods. They go to England.

Admiralty Court 4 of 36

  • ×4 Admiralty Court! The court checks your trade log. Any mistake: England takes the whole cargo. Free Passage can’t stop it.

Questions and answers (1 of 4)

What if we don’t have a ship?
Hire one or trade for one (see Ships). In Negotiation, only teams with a ship may send their Merchant out, so other Merchants will come to you.
Do we have to follow the triangle?
No. A ship can sail between any two ports.
Can we trade with England directly?
Yes. England is a port like the others.

Questions and answers (2 of 4)

Can we trade for something we don’t need?
Yes. Sometimes you get a good so you can trade it again for something you do need.
Can the Merchant and the Captain both leave?
No. Only one of them is away from port at a time.
What if we lose goods on a chance card?
The Captain picks which goods from the ship. A Free Passage card can cancel it. Chance cards never take a ship.

Questions and answers (3 of 4)

What if the Dock’s count and ours are different?
The Dock’s count is the official one. Tell the teacher if you think it is wrong.
Why write every trade in the log?
The Admiralty Court can check it. A mistake means England takes the whole cargo.
What happens with rum in New England?
Follow this rule: “Rum rule: must hold 2 molasses before each 1 rum may be traded.” The Harbormasters and the teacher check it.

Questions and answers (4 of 4)

Who wins if nobody finishes?
The team with the most of its needs list. A tie goes to the team with more voyages.
Why did the teacher stop the game?
Sometimes the teacher pauses the game to ask the whole class a question. That’s part of the game. Each trading day also ends with a few minutes on the standings.
Can we tell other teams what we need?
You can, but be careful. Your needs list is TOP SECRET. If others know what you need most, they can ask for more.

The history behind the game

This game scores goods. The real Triangle Trade also traded people.

On the second leg of the trade, ships carried enslaved African people across the Atlantic Ocean by force. That crossing is called the Middle Passage. Many people died on the way.

The sugar, tobacco, rice and indigo in this game were grown by enslaved people. They were forced to work and were never paid.

We’ll hold the game and the history together in the debrief.

Teacher notes

Shown only with ?teacher in the address. Not part of the board panels; the student PDF leaves it out.

Pause points

  • After Round 2 on the first trading day: press B (Curtain) on the Dock to cover the board, then a 2–3 minute whole-class check:
    • Which good is everyone chasing?
    • Why can’t every region finish?
    • Who holds the power, and where does it come from?
  • End of each trading day: about 5 minutes on the standings.

Likely misunderstandings, and what to say

“England always wins.” / “This is unfair.”
That’s the point. Ask why the system favored England: a monopoly on manufactured goods, the most ships (8), and duties paid to it.
“No one will trade with us.” (usually the Middle Colonies)
True to history: food and lumber were plentiful. Ask what they could carry or broker instead.
“We traded a lot, so we did well.”
Trading isn’t winning. The score is the share of needs secured.
“The game was fun, so the trade was good.”
That’s the debrief’s job: the scoring left out who did the work, and the people carried on the second leg.

Debrief plan

  • Open the debrief circle in the last ~10 minutes of the second trading day, while the results are fresh.
  • The next day (short, early release) is the written CER: Was the Triangle Trade worth it, and to whom?

Rules the Dock doesn’t enforce

  • The rum rule (“Rum rule: must hold 2 molasses before each 1 rum may be traded.”). The game shows it on New England’s card but doesn’t check it.
  • Payment for a hired ship: the fee rides as cargo. Load the fee goods in the hold with the rest (they count toward the limit). If the voyage sails to the ship’s owner, the Dock delivers the fee with everything else. If it sails somewhere else, leave the fee out of the Dock’s cargo: the Captain hands those cards to the owner’s port at the end of the voyage, and you move them with Log » Adjust Goods.
  • A traded ship card moves only when you use Log » Transfer Ship.
